segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a man from among the Pharisees, Nicodemus by name, a ruler of the Jews.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came to Jesus by night and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly I tell you, unless someone is born from above, they cannot see the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nicodemus said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How can a person be born when they are old? Surely they cannot enter their mother’s womb a second time and be born?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly I tell you, unless someone is born of water and Spirit, they cannot enter the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not be amazed that I told you, ‘You must all be born from above.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nicodemus answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How can these things happen?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are the teacher of Israel, and you do not understand these things?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly, truly I tell you, we speak of what we know and testify to what we have seen, yet you people do not accept our testimony.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If I have told you all about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God loved the world in this way: he gave his one and only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God did not send the Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has been judged already, because they have not believed in the name of the one and only Son of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light, because their deeds were evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For everyone who does what is base hates the light and does not come to the light, so that their deeds may not be exposed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that their deeds may be shown to have been done in God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and there he spent time with them and was baptizing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was plenty of water there, and people were coming and being baptized.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For John had not yet been thrown into prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a dispute arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew about purification.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to John and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, the one you have testified about—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “A person cannot receive a single thing unless it has been given to them from heaven.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You yourselves are my witnesses that I said, ‘I am not the Messiah,’ but, ‘I have been sent ahead of him.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the bridegroom’s friend, who stands and listens for him, is full of joy at the bridegroom’s voice. So this joy of mine is now complete.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He must increase, and I must decrease.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth. The one who comes from heaven is above all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He testifies to what he has seen and heard, yet no one accepts his testimony.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever has accepted his testimony has certified that God is true.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one whom God sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever disobeys the Son will not see life; rather, the wrath of God remains on them.

notes.note: The Greek word can mean either “from above” or “again,” and the dialogue plays on both: Nicodemus hears “a second time” (verse 4), while Jesus goes on to speak of birth from the Spirit. “From above” is chosen because that is the word’s meaning everywhere else in John, including verse 31 of this chapter. “Born again” is the traditional rendering and remains a legitimate reading; many scholars think the double meaning is deliberate.

notes.phrase: The wind blows where it wishes
notes.note: One Greek word means both “wind” and “spirit,” and the word for “sound” also means “voice.” The sentence can therefore also be heard as “The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice.” English cannot hold both; “wind” is used here because the saying works as a comparison, but the same word is translated “Spirit” at the end of the verse.
Many later manuscripts add “who is in heaven” after “the Son of Man.” The earliest witnesses lack the phrase, and the Greek text translated here omits it, though some scholars defend it as original.

The reference is to Numbers 21:4–9, where Moses set a bronze snake on a pole and those bitten by snakes looked at it and lived. The Greek verb means both to raise physically and to exalt; John uses it of Jesus’s crucifixion understood as his exaltation (compare 8:28 and 12:32–33).

The adjective is formed from the word for “age.” In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. In John this life is something the believer already has (verse 36).

notes.phrase: may have eternal life in him
notes.traditional: whosoever believeth in him should … have eternal life
notes.note: “In him” can be attached either to “believes” or to “have eternal life.” John normally uses a different preposition for “believe in,” as in verse 16, so the phrase is taken here with “have eternal life.” Many translations read “everyone who believes in him.”

Ancient manuscripts have no quotation marks, and it is unclear where Jesus’s words to Nicodemus end. This translation closes the speech at verse 15 and takes verses 16–21 as the evangelist’s own reflection, as many scholars and several modern versions do. Others continue Jesus’s speech through verse 21.

notes.traditional: For God so loved the world, that he gave
notes.note: The Greek adverb most often means “in this way,” pointing to how God loved: by giving his Son. The traditional “so loved” is now usually heard as “loved so much.” That sense of degree is also possible with the result clause that follows and is defended by many scholars, so the choice is disputed.

The word describes someone or something that is the only one of its kind, and was commonly used of an only child. Its second element is related to “kind,” not to “beget.” “One and only” is the mainstream modern rendering, though a minority of scholars have recently defended “only begotten.”

Most English versions use “condemn” in verses 17–18 and “judgment” or “verdict” in verse 19. The Greek uses one word family throughout, and “judge” and “judgment” keep that link visible. The context makes plain that an adverse judgment is meant, which is why “condemn” is the common rendering.

Some early manuscripts read the plural, “with Jews,” which older English versions follow. The singular is the reading of the Greek text translated here and is preferred by most editors. The identity of this person and the precise point in dispute are not stated.

The Greek word translates the Hebrew for “anointed one,” the title of the king Israel expected. Where it is a title under discussion, as here, this translation uses “Messiah.” Where it functions as a name alongside “Jesus,” it uses “Christ.” Several modern translations make the same distinction.

notes.phrase: The one who comes from above
notes.note: As at verse 16, it is unclear who is speaking. This translation ends John the Baptist’s words at verse 30 and treats verses 31–36 as the evangelist’s comment, since they echo the language of verses 11–21. Others take them as the continuation of John’s speech.

notes.phrase: he gives the Spirit without measure
notes.traditional: for God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him
notes.note: The Greek does not name the giver or the recipient. Most interpreters understand that God gives the Spirit without limit to the one he sent; the alternative is that the one sent gives the Spirit without limit to others. Some manuscripts add “God” as the subject to settle the question.

candidates.reason: Jesus’s formula “Amen (amen) I say to you” recurs throughout the Gospels and is rendered variously as “truly,” “very truly,” “verily,” “amen,” or “I tell you the truth”; readers should see one form.
Translators alternate between “judge” and “condemn” (and “judgment,” “verdict,” “condemnation” for κρίσις) across John, Paul and elsewhere, obscuring a single word family.
Capitalization (Spirit versus spirit) and the choice among wind, breath and spirit are interpretive decisions that recur across the whole New Testament and need a consistent policy.
The verb and its noun μαρτυρία are a key theme in John, Acts and Revelation and are variously rendered “testify,” “bear witness” and “witness”; consistency lets readers follow the theme.
Versions divide between “disobey,” “reject” and “not believe” wherever the word occurs (John, Acts, Romans, Hebrews, 1 Peter), and the choice affects how faith and obedience are related.
